data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["A formal proof checker is deterministic and stateless; an LLM verifier is stochastic and stateful, so its prior can introduce errors a deterministic checker would not.","Two engines may share training data even with different training histories, so engine separation alone does not guarantee prior decorrelation."],"overturn_conditions":["A population study showing same-engine verification catches injected false claims at the same rate as cross-engine verification would overturn the necessity claim.","Demonstration of a single-engine architecture whose verification module's error distribution is statistically independent of its generation module's error distribution would also overturn it."],"shared_structure":["A producer and a verifier share a common cause (training history / proof system version).","Verification that routes through the same common cause inherits its blind spots.","Genuine independence requires the verifier's error mode to be decorrelated from the producer's."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001","SRC_002"],"transfer_claims":["Same-engine self-checking inherits the engine's systematic bias just as same-version proof checking inherits the proof system's unsoundness.","Distinguishing genuine verification from restatement requires showing the checker's verdict is sensitive to evidence the author did not generate."]},"claim":"Separating the authoring engine from the checking engine is necessary for independent verification: an engine cannot catch its own systematic blind spots because its generative prior and its verification prior are the same distribution, so same-engine 'checking' is sample-dependent restatement rather than independent confirmation.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the claim is decided by a deterministic oracle (count, execution) whose output the engine cannot override, the oracle is the independent verifier even inside a single engine; engine separation is not necessary in that subcase.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a single-engine frozen-module architecture is shown to have priors whose errors are uncorrelated with the generative module's errors, it would meet the independence requirement without engine separation.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"An engine's prior assigns high probability to claims it is likely to generate. When it evaluates its own claim, it revisits the same hypothesis region it already deemed plausible, so it cannot detect any error that lies inside that region's support; genuine independence requires the checker's prior to put different mass on that region. Only a second training history supplies that difference.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
